explanations.explanation: A denarius for the day. That's the deal the landowner makes with the early crew (Matthew 20:2). Notice the pay is named up front. Hold on to that agreement, because it matters later.

A week would be a real long shift, friend. The text says he agreed to pay them a denarius "…for the day…" (Matthew 20:2). One day, one denarius. I'd be tired just reading about a week of vineyard work.
A month? That's a long stretch. The landowner agrees on a denarius "…for the day…" (Matthew 20:2). The pay is named for the day, and it's settled before anybody is sent into the vineyard.

explanations.answer: I will pay you whatever is right
explanations.explanation: He says, "…I will pay you whatever is right." (Matthew 20:4) Notice he doesn't name a number this time. So they go in with only that promise (Matthew 20:5). Keep that in mind when the evening comes.

explanations.answer: I will pay you half the day's wage
explanations.explanation: Half a wage is a fair guess, since they're starting later. But the landowner never says that. He says, "…I will pay you whatever is right." (Matthew 20:4) No fraction, no number, just a promise to do right.

explanations.answer: I will pay you once the harvest is in
explanations.explanation: Waiting on the harvest would be a long wait for a paycheck. Nothing like that shows up in the text. The landowner says, "…I will pay you whatever is right." (Matthew 20:4) And the pay comes when evening comes (Matthew 20:8).

True! The text says he went out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour and did the same thing (Matthew 20:5). Same man, same marketplace, same invitation. This guy has a hiring routine, and I respect it.

This one's actually true. The landowner goes out again about the sixth hour and the ninth hour and does the same thing (Matthew 20:5). He's back at that marketplace over and over. Somebody get this man a loyalty card.

Hired is right. They answer, "Because no one has hired us…" (Matthew 20:7) That's the reason they give for standing around. And I know something about waiting for somebody to come open the junk drawer I got stuck in.
Trusted is a good-sounding word, but it isn't theirs. They say, "Because no one has hired us…" (Matthew 20:7) Nobody had offered them work. That's the whole reason they were standing there.
Warned would make this a whole different story, friend. The workers say, "Because no one has hired us…" (Matthew 20:7) Hired is the word they use. That's the reason they give for standing there.
True. He tells them, "You also go into my vineyard…" (Matthew 20:7) The day is almost over and he still sends them in. I think those workers were mighty surprised to hear it.
Not false, friend. After they explain that no one hired them, he tells them, "You also go into my vineyard…" (Matthew 20:7) Late in the day, and the door is still open.

That's the order. The owner says to pay them "…starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first." (Matthew 20:8) So the late crew is first in line for the money. The first hired come last.

First to last sounds tidy, but that's not his order. He says, "…starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first." (Matthew 20:8) The last ones hired are paid first. The first hired are paid last.

One big pay line would be tidy, but that's not what he orders. He says, "…starting with the last ones hired and moving on to the first." (Matthew 20:8) There's an order, and it starts with the last hired.

A full denarius, each one. The text says the workers hired about the eleventh hour "…each received a denarius." (Matthew 20:9) An hour of work and a whole day's pay. I'd be checking the envelope twice.
Half would've seemed fair for a short shift. But the text says each of them "…received a denarius." (Matthew 20:9) The whole thing. The landowner didn't cut it in half.
A tenth, for about an hour of work? That's a crumb, and this landowner doesn't hand out crumbs. Each of them "…received a denarius." (Matthew 20:9) A full day's pay.

I get why you'd say that, because they assumed they'd get more (Matthew 20:10). But assuming isn't the same as getting. The text says "…each of them also received a denarius." (Matthew 20:10) The pay matched the deal.

False is right. They assumed they would receive more, but "…each of them also received a denarius." (Matthew 20:10) The same pay as the late crew, and the same as the deal they agreed on (Matthew 20:2).
Grumble is the word. The text says "…they began to grumble against the landowner." (Matthew 20:11) They did it on receiving their pay. I think we've all grumbled over a paycheck at some point.

Landowner is the one they grumbled against. The text says "…they began to grumble against the landowner." (Matthew 20:11) He's the man who made the deal with them (Matthew 20:2). The grumbling is aimed at him.
Rebel sounds dramatic, like they grabbed pitchforks. The text is calmer: "…they began to grumble against the landowner." (Matthew 20:11) Grumbling is more like muttering in the pay line.

The foreman is the one the owner tells to call the workers and pay them (Matthew 20:8). But the grumbling goes elsewhere: "…they began to grumble against the landowner." (Matthew 20:11) It's aimed at the landowner, not the foreman.
Plot makes it sound like a secret scheme, friend. The text says they "…began to grumble against the landowner." (Matthew 20:11) Grumble is the word, not plot. The text doesn't call it a scheme.
That's what he reminds him of. "Did you not agree with me on one denarius?" (Matthew 20:13) He calls him "Friend" first. The deal was made at the start, and the pay matched it.

explanations.answer: He was paid the day before
explanations.explanation: Yesterday's pay never comes up. The landowner says, "Did you not agree with me on one denarius?" (Matthew 20:13) He points back to the deal they made that very morning.

explanations.answer: He was warned about the heat
explanations.explanation: The workers do mention the scorching heat (Matthew 20:12). But the landowner never says he warned them about it. He asks, "Did you not agree with me on one denarius?" (Matthew 20:13) His point is the agreement.

explanations.answer: Are you envious because I am generous
explanations.explanation: That's the question. "Or are you envious because I am generous?" (Matthew 20:15) It lands right on the heart of the matter. The landowner says he is generous, and he gets to be.

explanations.answer: Are you tired because the day was long
explanations.explanation: The workers did talk about the long, hot day (Matthew 20:12). But that isn't his question. He asks, "Or are you envious because I am generous?" (Matthew 20:15)

explanations.answer: Are you angry because the work was hard
explanations.explanation: The hard work was their complaint (Matthew 20:12), but he doesn't ask about it. His question is, "Or are you envious because I am generous?" (Matthew 20:15) He asks about envy instead.
